About
Five Places, Five Questions

Every place I have worked has taught me to ask a better question.

1
Oman

“What really happens on a construction site?”

I walked into university already asking to be on a construction site. Curiosity opened the gate: I asked, got approval, and stayed, watching how things were really built. Before my degree was finished I was supervising on site, and after my first two years I was hired as an engineer. Research ran alongside all of it.

At Muscat Laboratory I learned the rule that still guides me: never trust the surface. Before anything is built, someone has to find out what the ground will really do. On projects like the Muscat International Airport Expansion, that someone was me.

The same rule found me outside the lab too. For years I had walked past the street cafés where Bangladeshi workers gathered, and I thought I knew what those places were. When I supported fieldwork and sat down to listen, I learned they were living rooms for people with no room to live in, and job boards without any paper. I had been familiar with the place. I had never understood it.

2
Bangladesh

“Can a dream carry its own weight?”

ZAP Comfortable Homes began as a dream: homes built around the people who live in them. I moved to Bangladesh to look beyond the Gulf, to understand the Asian market and to find out whether that dream could stand on its own. It could. Today it runs with a 32-member team, and I lead its operations.

The business taught me that the brief is rarely the real problem. One family came to us worried about their child's screen time. Instead of trying to change the child's habits, we changed the room: a full wall to draw on, shelves at the child's height, every surface safe. Within two weeks, their child was drawing every day.

Beyond the business, I kept asking questions, and followed some of them through independent research with the Engineering Society of Bangladesh.

3
Germany

“How do you turn a question into evidence?”

Germany was a deliberate choice. I wanted a formal degree in international project management, a closer understanding of the European construction industry, and to stay connected to different projects while I developed as a researcher.

At HFT Stuttgart I put a question from practice to the test: what actually carries a construction team through a crisis? I invited 350 practitioners to take part in a survey, and 92 responded. Nine of them gave me an hour each in in-depth interviews, speaking openly about what happens when a project begins to fail. I analysed every transcript by hand, in two full passes. The pattern was clear: teams that shared decision-making across levels held up better under mounting uncertainty than teams that relied on a single strong leader.

In Germany, I also joined EZBET e.V. as a member and volunteer.

4
Oman & Lisbon

“For whom?”

My fieldwork now follows people who move for work, in Oman and in Lisbon. In Lisbon, some people first told us the same thing: there is no housing. We kept talking, mapping and observing, and the picture became more uneven. Homes existed, but not everyone could find them, reach them or secure them.

The question changed from “Is there housing?” to “For whom, and how?”. Two words, and it became a different study.

5
Next

“Who decides?”

Construction sites, a laboratory, a business, a thesis, fieldwork: different places, but one question keeps returning. When things change faster than the plan, who gets to decide, and do they know enough to decide well? I am ready to follow that question further, on a construction project or in doctoral research.

Al Amerat Road Expansion — Site Engineer

Infrastructure delivery leaves no room for casual quality control. Every day started before the crew — site readiness, equipment checks, safety walk. Muscat Laboratory · Structural Assessment

Building Evaluation & Crack Monitoring Programme

Deteriorating concrete. Cracks across multiple floors. Owners who needed answers, not reassurance. Every evaluation followed a structured four-stage protocol: visual inspection; Schmidt Rebound Hammer NDT testing; concrete core extraction tested for compressive strength, carbonation depth, and chloride penetration; and crack survey with tell-tale monitoring.

HFT Stuttgart · MEng Research

Leading Through Crisis — Master's Thesis

This research explored what leadership capabilities actually matter when a construction project faces crisis. A structured literature review, a bilingual survey of construction practitioners (350 approached, 92 responses) and nine semi-structured interviews with project managers, a CEO and a senior site engineer, analysed through manual thematic analysis, identified the competencies that define pre-crisis readiness, active crisis response, and post-crisis recovery. A central finding: teams that spread decision-making capacity across levels proved more resilient under compounding uncertainty than teams run by strong individual leaders.

Crisis ManagementLeadership CompetencyStrategic ThinkingRisk ManagementResearch DesignAnalytical Thinking
HFT Stuttgart · MEng thesis · Thesis grade 1.7 (German scale, 1.0 = best)

Research
How I Research

What I study, how I think, and how I choose the right method for the question.

Research Focus

My core interest is distributed decision-making in construction project teams: how decision-making capacity is spread across levels of a team, and why that shapes how projects cope with crisis, uncertainty and change.

Around that core sit leadership and organisational behaviour, risk and crisis management, and the implementation of sustainable and circular construction. My methods are qualitative and mixed: surveys, semi-structured interviews and thematic analysis, grounded in ten years of construction practice across four countries.

Research
Independent Research Work

Sole-authored pre-prints. Each link opens the full paper.

Pre-print

Leadership Skills for Crisis Management in the German Construction Industry: A Mixed-methods Study

Combines a literature review, a practitioner survey and interviews to identify the leadership skills that matter when construction projects face crisis. Communication, decision-making and strategic planning rank highest, and the right mix of skills shifts across the pre-crisis, response and recovery stages.

DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7241638Read paper →
Pre-print

Crisis Management Strategies and Organizational Challenges in the Construction Industry: A Structured Review with Practitioner Insights

A structured literature review read alongside interviews with construction professionals in Germany. It maps three staged crisis-management models and five strategic approaches, and identifies financial volatility, communication breakdown across stakeholders and a shortage of structured training as the main organisational obstacles.

DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7242178Read paper →
Pre-print

Developing Crisis Leadership in Construction: The Role of Structured Training, Reflection, and Organizational Learning

Examines how crisis leadership capability is built inside construction organisations, drawing on interviews with professionals in Germany. It argues that crisis leadership is an organisational asset developed through cycles of post-crisis reflection, knowledge capture and structured training, not only an individual trait.

DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7242619Read paper →
Pre-print

Leadership Skills for Crisis Management in the Construction Industry: A Self-, Business- and People-Management Categorization

Tests ten candidate leadership skills through a bilingual survey of 92 construction professionals and groups them into self-, business- and people-management domains. Business-focused skills dominate before and during a crisis, people skills lead in recovery, and communication and accountability matter throughout.

DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21892978Read paper →
Pre-print

Comparative Effect of Compaction Energy on Lime- and GGBS-Stabilised Fine Soil: A Laboratory Investigation

A laboratory study of fine soil stabilised with varying proportions of lime and ground granulated blast furnace slag (GGBS) under different compaction energies. Both stabilisers raised maximum dry density and lowered optimum moisture content, with GGBS giving the greater density gain.

DOI 10.2139/ssrn.7242118Read paper →
Pre-print

Effect of Lime and Ground Granulated Blast Furnace Slag on the Compaction Behaviour of Fine Soil: Full Experimental Report

The full experimental report behind the lime and GGBS stabilisation study, documenting the laboratory programme, test procedures and compaction results in detail.

DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21893706Read paper →
Research
Ongoing Independent Research

Self-directed inquiries arising from my professional practice, which I am developing towards formal research.

Ongoing

Client Decision-Making and Behavioural Preference Patterns in Residential Interior Design

Observing patterns in how clients across the ZAP portfolio make decisions, weigh trade-offs, and express aesthetic and budget preferences, with a view to what these patterns suggest at the level of the business as a whole.

Ongoing

Understanding Client Psychology in Bespoke Residential Interior Delivery

Exploring how an individual client's motivations, priorities, and anxieties unfold over the course of a single bespoke project, informing how I manage that relationship directly.

Ongoing

Direct-Access Market Structures: Understanding Wholesaler-Retailer-Client Relationships in Bangladesh

Examining how the Bangladeshi construction materials market's unusual pattern of direct client access to wholesalers reshapes the traditional roles of retailers and intermediaries, and what that means for how a construction business should be positioned commercially.
